```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source('../assets/setup.R')
```

A "package" in R is a collection of code that someone out there in the R community wrote.
Packages are usually designed for specific purposes.

For example:

- `tidyverse`: designed for wrangling data
- `skimr`: designed for previewing data
- `cowsay`: a silly little package that prints out an ASCII cartoon (see below!)

We install a package only once.
But each time we start writing in a new R script, we have to load the packages we need.  

![](images/rstudio_intro/libraries.jpeg)


## To install a package

In the __console__ (not in your R script), type `install.packages("cowsay")` and hit Enter.
  
Lots of red text will come up, and it will take a bit of time. 

When it has finished, and R is ready for you to use again, you will see the blue sign >. 


## To load a package

In your R script (not in the console), type `library(cowsay)` and run the line.
This *loads* the package for us to use it.

(Why do we load the script in the R script and not the console?
We include all `library()` lines in our R script (rather than running them in the console) so that anyone else who tries to run our code knows what R packages we have used in this specific script.)

```{r}
library(cowsay)
```


## To use a package

After running `library(cowsay)`, you have access to all the contents of the package `cowsay`.
Here's an example.

In the next line of your R script, type `say("hello world", by = "cow")` and run the line.
Hopefully you got a similar result to ours:  

```{r}
say("hey there!", by = "cow")
```

Then why not try this in the next line?

```{r}
say("what's up?", by = 'grumpycat')
```


## Errors if package not loaded

If you tried to run that line of code without running `library(cowsay)` first, R would give you an error message:

```
Error in say("what's up?", by = "grumpycat") : 
  could not find function "say"
```

If you think your code should work and the error says something like "could not find function", then chances are that you've either left out or forgotten to run the line that loads that package.
